1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4 Bxb4 5..strategy: Hits the bishop again and prepares to build a centre with d4, so the bishop must move for a second time. This is the point of the gambit: White gives a pawn for time and a pawn centre, and the queen also gets the b3 square, aiming at f7 together with the bishop.

The main retreat: the bishop stays on the diagonal to e1, so once White plays d4 the c3 pawn is pinned and cannot simply recapture. It keeps the pawn and sets the sharpest test of the gambit, but takes a5 away from the knight.

The safest retreat: the bishop cannot be hit again soon, covers g5 and helps the king, and leaves a5 free for the knight to challenge the bishop on c4. Black often returns the pawn later and aims for a solid, balanced game.
Adds a defender to e5, so that d4 no longer arrives with an attack on the pawn. The price is that the bishop blocks the d-pawn. A solid, less trodden way to keep the extra pawn for now.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4 Bxb4 5..name: Italian Game: Evans Gambit, Stone-Ware Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4 Bxb4 5..background: Named after Henry Nathan Stone and Preston Ware. Grandmasters including Andrei Volokitin, Alexander Grischuk and Loek van Wely have played it.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4 Bxb4 5..strategy: Goes back to the square it came from in the hope of stopping d4, but White plays it anyway with tempo on the bishop. Black has spent three bishop moves to keep one pawn, and White has a free hand in the centre.

Undevelops the bishop completely: Black has spent three moves to win a pawn with it and, to castle, must now move it again as well as bring out the g8 knight. White takes the centre with a large lead in development.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4 Bxb4 5..name: Italian Game: Evans Gambit, Mayet Defence
